guide.title: Pinnacle Ski Club, Maine: Pittsfield's Kiwanis-founded hill since 1954
guide.intro: Per New England Ski History's Pinnacle Ski Club page, in the early 1950s former Bowdoin ski team member Jack Baxter and PSIA instructor Byron "Bud" Dow "were troubled by the lack of opportunities for local youngsters to learn to ski"; in the fall of 1954 the two "worked with an elderly property owner and the local Kiwanis to develop a small ski area on the eastern slope of an area known as the Pinnacle." Through the hard work and donations of many local residents, the area, known as the "Kiwanis Community Ski Slopes," was open by early winter of 1954 and served by a rope tow, at a $1.00 lift ticket price.

sections.heading: Dozens of kids a day
sections.body: By the end of the first (1954-55) season, per the same source, "dozens of kids a day were taking part in ski school classes." "Over the next decade, the property likely ended up in the hands of the Town of Pittsfield and the Maine Central Institute." The area grew to feature "open slopes on either side of the rope tow, a steep race course into a gravel pit, and a ski jump between the slope and the race course." Instructor and co-founder Bud Dow died in 1979.

sections.heading: Operated by the club, open to the public
sections.body: The New England Lost Ski Areas Project corroborates that the area was "operated by the local Kiwanis Club, then by the Pinnacle Ski Club" and "continues to be operated today when snowfalls permit." Per New England Ski History, the area "has remained in operation, operated by the Pinnacle Ski Club," with two rope tows, no snowmaking, but night skiing offered; the adult weekend full-day ticket for 2025-26 is $20.00. The club's own website lists both membership options (Single $40.00, Family $100.00 for 5 immediate family members) and separate public day tickets (Single Day Pass $20.00, Family Day Pass $50.00), confirming day tickets are sold to the public alongside memberships. The club's own site also advertises "Learn to ski, snowboard, and Race all for Free!" as part of its public-facing program.

sections.heading: Hours and mission
sections.body: The club's own site frames its mission as "Promoting and encouraging skiing for Pittsfield residents and the surrounding communities," inviting the public to "Come join great family fun!" Public ski hours are Friday Night Ski 6:00-9:00 p.m. and Saturday-Sunday 10:00 a.m.-4:00 p.m., "(Times and dates are subject to change due to weather and volunteers)." The club's own site states it has "operated the ski slope for more than 65 years."

sections.heading: In Pittsfield
sections.body: "The Pittsfield Historical Society was formed in 1983 in a community effort to preserve and protect some of the town's most valuable assets: its history and artifacts," per the society's own website. The society meets at "the Depot House Museum on Central Street," housed in the original 1886 Pittsfield Railroad Depot and open by appointment, where "the public is always welcome to join us." Manson Park was donated to the Town of Pittsfield by John W. Manson in 1926 (the first section, during his lifetime) and 1941 (a second section, by bequest), per the Pittsfield Historical Society's Manson Park page. Manson's will stated his wishes: "I desire it to be improved, beautified and, if necessary, enlarged, to be used somewhat, not principally, as a sport field to which the students of Maine Central Institute shall be welcome; to be used especially as a garden, walk, and playground for all the people."

faq.question: Is Pinnacle Ski Club open to the public, despite the name?
faq.answer: Yes. Per the club's own website, it sells single and family day passes ($20.00 and $50.00 for 2025-26) alongside memberships, and New England Ski History's ticket table independently confirms the same public $20.00 day rate.

faq.question: Who founded Pinnacle Ski Club?
faq.answer: Former Bowdoin ski team member Jack Baxter and PSIA instructor Byron "Bud" Dow, who worked with the local Kiwanis club in the fall of 1954 to develop the hill, per New England Ski History's Pinnacle Ski Club page.

places.name: Depot House Museum
places.summary: A local history museum housed in Pittsfield's original 1886 railroad depot, run by the Pittsfield Historical Society.
places.history: "The Pittsfield Historical Society was formed in 1983 in a community effort to preserve and protect some of the town's most valuable assets: its history and artifacts," per the society's own website. The society "collects bits and pieces of Pittsfield history largely through donated artifacts, photographs, newspapers, family scrapbooks and diaries," meeting at "the Depot House Museum on Central Street," where "the public is always welcome to join us." The museum is housed in the original Pittsfield Railroad Depot, built in 1886, and is open by appointment, per TravelMaine.com's Depot House Museum listing.

places.name: Manson Park
places.summary: A town park in Pittsfield donated by lawyer John W. Manson, home to the annual Central Maine Egg Festival.
places.history: Manson Park was donated to the Town of Pittsfield by John W. Manson, "a prestigious Pittsfield lawyer and businessman," and named for his mother; per the Pittsfield Historical Society's Manson Park page, the first and largest section was donated in 1926 during his lifetime, with a second section transferred upon his death in 1941 as a bequest in his will. Manson's will stated his wishes for the park: "I desire it to be improved, beautified and, if necessary, enlarged, to be used somewhat, not principally, as a sport field to which the students of Maine Central Institute shall be welcome; to be used especially as a garden, walk, and playground for all the people." Construction of the park commenced in 1946 and it was opened officially in 1948-49, per the same source; the park now serves as headquarters for the annual Central Maine Egg Festival and Kiwanis Karnival.
